claim: CPSF30 depletion causes profound and general transcriptional read-through downstream of protein-coding genes.
source: This results in profound and general transcriptional read-through downstream of protein-coding genes (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) demonstrating widespread impairment of PAS function.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing increased transcription downstream of protein-coding genes following CPSF30 depletion, as shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: ZC3H4 and ZC3H6 were the most depleted factors after CPSF complex components in the mTurbo proximity labeling experiment following CPSF30 depletion.
source: Two poorly characterised factors, ZC3H4 and ZC3H6, were the next most depleted.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from the mTurbo proximity labeling experiment shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ZC3H4 interacts with WDR82.
source: Although little is reported on ZC3H4, two independent studies uncovered it as an interaction partner of WDR82 using mass spectrometry (Lee et al., 2010; van Nuland et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: ZC3H4 and ZC3H6 are largely restricted to metazoans and are paralogues.
source: Although WDR82 is conserved between human and budding yeast, our phylogenetic analysis suggested that ZC3H4 and ZC3H6 are largely restricted to metazoans and are paralogues (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: ZC3H4 loss has a more noticeable impact on transcription than ZC3H6 depletion.
source: Comparison of these datasets shows that ZC3H4 loss has a more noticeable impact than ZC3H6 depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing the effects of ZC3H4 and ZC3H6 depletion shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ZC3H4 depletion causes upregulation and extension of PROMPT transcripts.
source: Figure 2C shows an example PROMPT, upstream of MYC, which is undetectable in control siRNA-treated cells, but abundant following ZC3H4 depletion. Loss of ZC3H4 also leads to the extension of this transcript by more than 100 kilobases.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing increased and extended PROMPT transcription at the MYC locus following ZC3H4 depletion, as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ZC3H4 depletion causes upregulation and extension of enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) at super-enhancers.
source: ZC3H4 depletion has a clear effect over SE regions exemplified by the MYC SE where upregulation and extension of eRNAs is obvious (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing increased eRNA transcription at super-enhancers following ZC3H4 depletion, as shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: ZC3H4 has a more substantial effect on PROMPT regions than Integrator depletion.
source: Where ZC3H4 effects are evident over PROMPT regions, they are generally more substantial than those seen after Integrator loss, exemplified by the ITPRID2 PROMPT in Figure 3F and via meta-analyses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data from ZC3H4 and INTS1 depletion experiments shown in Figure 3F and supplementary figures.

claim: ZC3H4 depletion results in greater stabilization and elongation of eRNA at super-enhancers compared to INTS1 knockdown.
source: At SEs, ZC3H4 depletion generally results in a greater stabilisation and elongation of eRNA, compared to INTS1 knockdown, exemplified at the MSRB3 SE (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data from ZC3H4 and INTS1 depletion experiments shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: Rapid ZC3H4 depletion using the DHFR degron system confirms the effects observed by RNAi are not due to compensatory pathways.
source: All were increased following ZC3H4 loss, suggesting that the effects that we observed by RNAi are not due to compensatory pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased PROMPT and SE transcripts following rapid (4 hr) ZC3H4 depletion using the DHFR degron system, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Re-administration of TMP to restore ZC3H4 levels reverses the effects of its depletion on PROMPT and SE transcripts.
source: Although 4 hr TMP re-administration does not restore ZC3H4 to full levels, it was sufficient to reverse the effects of its depletion at all tested amplicons.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing that ZC3H4 re-expression reverses the increase in PROMPT and SE transcripts, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Extended PROMPT transcripts resulting from ZC3H4 loss are due to aberrant transcription of these loci.
source: Rapid ZC3H4 depletion also confirmed the prediction, from our RNA-seq, that the extended PROMPT transcripts result from the aberrant transcription of these loci (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pol II ChIP data showing increased polymerase occupancy at PROMPT regions following ZC3H4 depletion, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WDR82 depletion enhances the level of PROMPT and SE transcripts tested.
source: WDR82 depletion enhanced the level of all tested transcripts suggesting that it functionally overlaps with ZC3H4 (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased PROMPT and SE transcripts following WDR82 depletion, as shown in Figure 4G.

claim: There is no synergistic effect of co-depleting ZC3H4 and WDR82, implying they do not act redundantly at the tested loci.
source: There was no synergistic effect of their co-depletion, implying that WDR82 and ZC3H4 do not act redundantly at the tested loci.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing that co-depletion of ZC3H4 and WDR82 does not further increase transcript levels beyond single depletions, as shown in Figure 4G.

claim: PP1 (PNUTS) but not SETD1A/B is implicated in the stability of the non-coding transcripts tested.
source: We found that the former but not the latter is implicated in the stability of the non-coding transcripts selected for this experiment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing that PNUTS depletion increases PROMPT and SE transcripts while SETD1A/B depletion does not, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: ZC3H4 occupies genes with binding broadly resembling that of Pol II and showing the greatest enrichment over promoter regions.
source: ZC3H4 occupies genes with binding broadly resembling that of Pol II and showing the greatest enrichment over promoter regions (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing ZC3H4 occupancy patterns similar to Pol II with enrichment at promoters, as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Many genes that are occupied by Pol II do not recruit ZC3H4.
source: However, many genes that are occupied by Pol II do not recruit ZC3H4 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing differential occupancy of genes by ZC3H4 compared to Pol II, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ZC3H4 occupies a broader promoter region than Pol II.
source: Interestingly, ZC3H4 occupies a broader promoter region than Pol II, suggesting that its function is not restricted to the precise transcriptional start site.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing broader ZC3H4 peaks compared to Pol II at promoters, as shown in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: ZC3H4 is strongly recruited to super-enhancers.
source: ZC3H4 is also strongly recruited to SEs consistent with the RNA effects observed on them following its loss (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing ZC3H4 occupancy at super-enhancers, as shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: ZC3H4 shows proportionally greater occupancy at distal intergenic regions (encompassing super-enhancers) compared to Pol II.
source: Although our analyses of eRNA and PROMPTs were guided by our RNA-seq findings, an unbiased search for peaks of ZC3H4 and Pol II signal confirmed proportionally greater ZC3H4 occupancy at distal intergenic regions (encompassing SEs) (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq peak analysis showing enrichment of ZC3H4 at distal intergenic regions, as shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ZC3H4 directly crosslinks to RNA in cells.
source: This might result from low affinity of the ZC3H4 antibody or that its recruitment to chromatin is bridged since ZC3H4 also directly crosslinks to RNA in cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by XRNAX data showing UV-dependent recovery of ZC3H4 with RNA, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Tethered ZC3H4-MS2 significantly reduces reporter RNA expression compared to controls.
source: Compared to the two controls, tethered ZC3H4-MS2 significantly reduced reporter RNA expression (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing reduced reporter RNA levels when ZC3H4-MS2 is tethered to the reporter, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ZC3H4-MS2 does not affect the same reporter lacking MS2 hairpins.
source: ZC3H4-MS2 expression does not affect the same reporter lacking MS2 hairpins (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing no effect of ZC3H4-MS2 on a reporter without MS2 hairpins, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ZC3H4 recruitment is sufficient to negatively regulate RNA expression.
source: This directly demonstrates that ZC3H4 recruitment is sufficient to negatively regulate RNA expression, mirroring the upregulation of its endogenous targets seen when it is depleted.
evidence: The claim is supported by tethered function assay data showing that ZC3H4-MS2 recruitment reduces reporter RNA levels, as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tethered ZC3H4 acts on nascent RNA.
source: This amplicon and that upstream of the MS2 hairpins were reduced in this chromatin fraction, strongly suggesting that tethered ZC3H4 acts on nascent RNA (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data on chromatin-associated RNA showing reduced reporter RNA levels when ZC3H4-MS2 is tethered, as shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Recruited ZC3H4 promotes the release of RNA that is a DIS3 substrate.
source: Enhanced levels of upstream versus downstream amplicon were associated with transfection of ZC3H4-MS2 and is more prominent after depletion of DIS3. This is consistent with the hypothesis that recruited ZC3H4 promotes the release of RNA that is a DIS3 substrate (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased upstream/downstream RNA ratio with ZC3H4-MS2 tethering, especially after DIS3 depletion, as shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Loss of ZC3H4 is associated with smaller colonies in colony formation assays, demonstrating its importance for growth/proliferation.
source: Loss of ZC3H4 was associated with smaller colonies, which demonstrates the importance of ZC3H4 for growth/proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data showing reduced colony size in the absence of ZC3H4, as shown in Figure 6F.

claim: ZC3H4 controls unproductive transcription, especially at non-coding loci.
source: We have discovered that ZC3H4 controls unproductive transcription, especially at non-coding loci.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and tethered function assays showing ZC3H4's role in restricting non-coding transcription.

claim: ZC3H4 recruitment drives some of the early transcriptional termination that is characteristic of many non-coding RNAs, particularly PROMPT and eRNA transcripts.
source: We propose that ZC3H4 recruitment drives some of the early transcriptional termination that is characteristic of many non-coding RNAs, particularly PROMPT and eRNA transcripts.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations including ZC3H4 occupancy at PROMPT and eRNA loci, and the effects of its depletion on these transcripts.

claim: The effects of ZC3H4 depletion are reminiscent of recent findings on the Integrator complex.
source: The effects of ZC3H4 depletion are reminiscent of recent findings on the Integrator complex, which also controls the early termination of transcription (Elrod et al., 2019; Lykke-Andersen et al., 2020; Tatomer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ZC3H4 and Integrator effects, with citations to previous studies on Integrator function.

claim: ZC3H4 and Integrator can act on separate RNA targets.
source: Our initial comparison of transcripts sensitive to either Integrator or ZC3H4 suggests that they can act on separate RNA targets.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing minimal overlap between transcripts affected by ZC3H4 versus Integrator depletion, as shown in Figure 3D and supplementary figures.

claim: ZC3H4 has been proposed as an equivalent to Drosophila Suppressor of Sable (Su(s)).
source: ZC3H4 has been proposed as an equivalent to Drosophila Suppressor of Sable (Su(s)), which negatively regulates transcription via promoter-proximal termination (Brewer-Jensen et al., 2016; Kuan et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Su(s) and comparison of its function to ZC3H4.

claim: ZC3H4 and Su(s) share little sequence homology, but they have similar structural makeup with zinc fingers flanked by largely disordered regions.
source: ZC3H4 and Su(s) share little sequence homology, but they have similar structural makeup with zinc fingers flanked by largely disordered regions.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of ZC3H4 and comparison to Su(s), as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Su(s) depletion stabilises selected RNAs and causes their aberrant elongation and stability, mirroring what is seen globally following ZC3H4 depletion.
source: Su(s) depletion stabilises selected RNAs and causes their aberrant elongation and stability, mirroring what we see globally following ZC3H4 depletion.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of ZC3H4 effects to published data on Su(s) function.

claim: WDR82 may be the only interacting partner of Su(s) according to IP and mass spectrometry.
source: Interestingly, IP and mass spectrometry indicate that WDR82 may be the only interacting partner of Su(s) (Brewer-Jensen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on Su(s) interactions.

claim: WDR82 has been shown to bind to Pol II phosphorylated on Serine 5 of its C-terminal domain.
source: WDR82 has been shown to bind to Pol II phosphorylated on Serine 5 of its C-terminal domain, which may provide a means to recruit ZC3H4 to promoter-proximal regions (Lee and Skalnik, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on WDR82 function.

claim: The recruitment of ZC3H4 to promoters is consistent with the observation that promoter-proximal transcription is most affected by its absence.
source: The recruitment of ZC3H4 to promoters is consistent with our observation that promoter-proximal transcription is most affected by its absence.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from ChIP-seq data showing ZC3H4 occupancy at promoters and RNA-seq data showing effects on promoter-proximal transcripts.

claim: ZC3H4 was proposed to terminate some non-coding transcripts as a result of spurious/weak splicing.
source: In agreement with our findings, non-coding transcripts were affected by ZC3H4 depletion. ZC3H4 was proposed to terminate some non-coding transcripts as a result of spurious/weak splicing.
evidence: The claim is based on citation to a recent study (Austenaa et al., 2021) that was published while this manuscript was under revision.

claim: Su(s) regulation of transcription was linked to the presence of a cryptic 5' splice site.
source: Similarly, Su(s) regulation of transcription was linked to the presence of a cryptic 5' splice site (Kuan et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on Su(s) function.

claim: U1 snRNA inhibition causes some stabilisation of PROMPTs, but does not generally result in their longer extension.
source: While U1 snRNA inhibition does cause some stabilisation of PROMPTs, it does not generally result in their longer extension and so other cis-acting sequences and processes may additionally contribute (Oh et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on U1 snRNA function.

claim: ZC3H4 binds RNA in cells.
source: Our evidence that ZC3H4 binds RNA in cells suggests that it may directly interact with some of its target transcripts and it will be important to delineate any sequence determinants.
evidence: The claim is supported by XRNAX data showing UV-dependent recovery of ZC3H4 with RNA, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ZC3H4 contains large regions of intrinsic disorder, which can promote phase separation properties.
source: While we do not know whether ZC3H4 can phase separate, it contains large regions of intrinsic disorder, which can promote this property (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of ZC3H4 showing disordered regions, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, and knowledge about the relationship between disorder and phase separation.

claim: CPSF30 is the first step of PAS recognition involving binding to the AAUAAA signal.
source: The first step of PAS recognition involves the binding of CPSF30 to the AAUAAA signal (Chan et al., 2014; Clerici et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on CPSF30 function.

claim: Termination of protein-coding transcription is coupled to 3' end processing of pre-mRNA via cleavage at the polyadenylation signal (PAS).
source: Termination of protein-coding transcription is coupled to 3' end processing of pre-mRNA via cleavage at the polyadenylation signal (PAS) (Eaton and West, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous review on transcriptional termination.

claim: A PAS consists of an AAUAAA hexamer followed by a U/GU-rich region.
source: A PAS consists of an AAUAAA hexamer followed by a U/GU-rich region (Proudfoot, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous review on polyadenylation signals.

claim: CPSF73 cleaves the nascent RNA and the Pol II-associated product is degraded 5'→3' by XRN2 to promote termination.
source: After assembly of a multi-protein processing complex, CPSF73 cleaves the nascent RNA and the Pol II-associated product is degraded 5'→3' by XRN2 to promote termination (Eaton et al., 2018; Eaton et al., 2020; Fong et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on transcriptional termination mechanisms.

claim: The Pol II elongation complex is modified as it crosses the PAS, which facilitates its termination by XRN2.
source: The Pol II elongation complex is modified as it crosses the PAS, which facilitates its termination by XRN2 (Cortazar et al., 2019; Eaton et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Pol II modification during termination.

claim: Depletion of XRN2 or CPSF73 causes read-through downstream of some long non-coding genes.
source: Depletion of XRN2 or CPSF73 causes read-through downstream of some long non-coding genes (Eaton et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on termination at non-coding genes.

claim: A substantial fraction of non-coding transcription is less sensitive to XRN2 or CPSF73 depletion suggesting the use of alternative mechanisms.
source: However, a substantial fraction of non-coding transcription is less sensitive to their depletion suggesting the use of alternative mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from previous studies showing that not all non-coding transcripts are affected by XRN2 or CPSF73 depletion.

claim: The Integrator complex aids termination of many non-coding transcripts, with the archetypal example being snRNAs.
source: The Integrator complex aids termination of many non-coding transcripts, with the archetypal example being snRNAs (Baillat et al., 2005; Davidson et al., 2020; O'Reilly et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Integrator function.

claim: Integrator is implicated in the termination of promoter upstream transcripts (PROMPTs) and enhancer RNAs (eRNAs).
source: Integrator is also implicated in the termination of promoter upstream transcripts (PROMPTs) and enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) (Beckedorff et al., 2020; Lai et al., 2015; Nojima et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Integrator function at PROMPTs and eRNAs.

claim: INTS11 activity does not precede XRN2 degradation at snRNA genes.
source: However, INTS11 activity does not precede XRN2 degradation at snRNA genes (Eaton et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on the timing of INTS11 and XRN2 activities.

claim: There is evidence of redundant pathways at snRNA loci for transcriptional termination.
source: Moreover, while CPSF73 is indispensable for termination at protein-coding genes, there is evidence of redundant pathways at snRNA loci (Davidson et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on termination mechanisms at snRNA genes.

claim: CPSF and the cap binding complex-associated factor, ARS2, are both implicated in the termination of promoter-proximal transcription.
source: Indeed, CPSF and the cap binding complex-associated factor, ARS2, are both implicated in the termination of promoter-proximal transcription (Iasillo et al., 2017; Nojima et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on CPSF and ARS2 function.

claim: Premature cleavage and polyadenylation (PCPA) can be controlled by U1 snRNA, CDK12, SCAF4/8, or PCF11.
source: Frequently, this is via premature cleavage and polyadenylation (PCPA) that can be controlled by U1 snRNA, CDK12, SCAF4/8, or PCF11 (Dubbury et al., 2018; Gregersen et al., 2019; Kaida et al., 2010; Kamieniarz-Gdula et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on factors controlling PCPA.

claim: PCPA is common on many genes since acute depletion of the exosome stabilises its predicted products in otherwise unmodified cells.
source: PCPA is common on many genes since acute depletion of the exosome stabilises its predicted products in otherwise unmodified cells (Chiu et al., 2018; Davidson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on PCPA and exosome function.

claim: Integrator activity attenuates transcription at hundreds of protein-coding genes.
source: Integrator activity also attenuates transcription at hundreds of protein-coding genes (Elrod et al., 2019; Tatomer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Integrator function at protein-coding genes.

claim: WDR82 forms at least two complexes in mammals: one with the SETD1 histone methyl-transferase and another composed of protein-phosphatase 1 and its nuclear targeting subunit PNUTS.
source: In mammals, WDR82 forms at least two complexes: one with the SETD1 histone methyl-transferase and another composed of protein-phosphatase 1 and its nuclear targeting subunit PNUTS (Lee et al., 2010; van Nuland et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on WDR82 complexes.

claim: A version of the WDR82-PP1-PNUTS complex promotes transcriptional termination in trypanosomes.
source: A version of the latter promotes transcriptional termination in trypanosomes (Kieft et al., 2020) and the budding yeast homologue of WDR82, Swd2, forms part of the APT (associated with Pta1) termination complex (Nedea et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on WDR82 function in trypanosomes and yeast.

claim: Depletion of either WDR82, PNUTS, or SET1 causes non-coding transcriptional termination defects in murine cells.
source: In murine cells, depletion of either WDR82, PNUTS, or SET1 causes non-coding transcriptional termination defects (Austenaa et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on WDR82, PNUTS, and SET1 function in mice.

claim: PNUTS/PP1 dephosphorylation of SPT5 causes deceleration of Pol II beyond the PAS.
source: Notably, PNUTS/PP1 is also implicated in the canonical termination pathway at protein-coding genes where its dephosphorylation of SPT5 causes deceleration of Pol II beyond the PAS (Cortazar et al., 2019; Eaton et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on PNUTS/PP1 function in termination.

claim: Most of the human genome can be transcribed by RNA polymerase II (Pol II).
source: Most of the human genome can be transcribed by RNA polymerase II (Pol II).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about genome-wide transcription.

claim: Long non-coding RNAs are broadly classified as greater than ~200 nucleotides in length.
source: Among these transcripts are thousands of long non-coding RNAs, broadly classified as greater than ~200 nucleotides in length (Kopp and Mendell, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous review on long non-coding RNAs.

claim: Most long non-coding RNAs are rapidly degraded by the exosome.
source: They share some structural features with coding transcripts, but most of them are rapidly degraded by the exosome (Davidson et al., 2019; Preker et al., 2008; Schlackow et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on exosome-mediated degradation of non-coding RNAs.

claim: Degradation of long non-coding RNAs is coincident with or shortly after transcriptional termination, which often occurs within a few kilobases.
source: Their degradation is coincident with or shortly after transcriptional termination, which often occurs within a few kilobases (kb).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the timing and location of non-coding RNA degradation.

claim: The mechanisms for terminating non-coding transcription are poorly understood, especially by comparison with those operating at protein-coding genes.
source: The mechanisms for terminating non-coding transcription are poorly understood, especially by comparison with those operating at protein-coding genes.
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: PROMPTs are normally rapidly degraded 3'→5' by the exosome.
source: These PROMPT transcripts are normally rapidly degraded 3'→5' by the exosome (Preker et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on PROMPT degradation.

claim: DIS3 depletion stabilises the usual extent of PROMPT RNA, which is much shorter than when ZC3H4 is absent.
source: DIS3 depletion stabilises the usual extent of PROMPT RNA, which is much shorter than when ZC3H4 is absent.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data from DIS3 and ZC3H4 depletion experiments, as shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: PROMPT transcripts are stabilised and extended in the absence of ZC3H4, presumably because its normal function restricts their transcription.
source: These data strongly suggest that PROMPT transcripts are stabilised and extended in the absence of ZC3H4, presumably because its normal function restricts their transcription.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from RNA-seq data showing increased and extended PROMPT transcripts following ZC3H4 depletion.

claim: eRNAs can be found in isolation and in clusters called super-enhancers (SEs).
source: eRNAs can be found in isolation and in clusters called super-enhancers (SEs) (Pott and Lieb, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous review on enhancer RNAs and super-enhancers.

claim: SEs are thought to be important for controlling key developmental genes with strong relevance to disease.
source: SEs are thought to be important for controlling key developmental genes with strong relevance to disease (Hnisz et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on super-enhancer function.

claim: PROMPTs susceptible to ZC3H4 were not enriched in PASs compared to those unaffected by it and harbour a slightly lower density.
source: Consistently, PROMPTs susceptible to ZC3H4 were not enriched in PASs compared to those unaffected by it and harbour a slightly lower density (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of PAS density in PROMPTs, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Integrator is a metazoan-specific assembly with regulatory functions at non-coding loci.
source: This is a metazoan-specific assembly with regulatory functions at non-coding loci (Lai et al., 2015; Mendoza-Figueroa et al., 2020; Nojima et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Integrator function.

claim: Integrator depletion can lead to increased expression of a subset of mRNAs.
source: Because of this function, Integrator depletion can lead to increased expression of a subset of mRNAs (Elrod et al., 2019; Lykke-Andersen et al., 2020; Tatomer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Integrator effects on mRNA expression.

claim: Around 1000 genes are affected by INTS1 or ZC3H4 depletion with little overlap between the two conditions.
source: Bioinformatic analysis revealed around 1000 genes affected by INTS1 or ZC3H4 depletion with little overlap between the two conditions (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data from INTS1 and ZC3H4 depletion experiments, as shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Analysis of recently published metabolically labelled RNA-seq data from HeLa cells depleted of the catalytic Integrator subunit or ZC3H4 reveals many upregulated mRNAs with minimal overlap.
source: Indeed, analysis of recently published metabolically labelled RNA-seq data from HeLa cells depleted of the catalytic Integrator subunit or ZC3H4 reveals many upregulated mRNAs – also with minimal overlap (Austenaa et al., 2021; Lykke-Andersen et al., 2020; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published data from other studies, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Transcripts upregulated following either ZC3H4 or INTS1 loss are normally expressed at lower levels than those from unaffected genes.
source: When searching for characteristics of these targets in our own RNA-seq data, we found that transcripts upregulated following either ZC3H4 or INTS1 loss are normally expressed at lower levels than those from unaffected genes (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of expression levels of upregulated transcripts, as shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Transcripts upregulated by ZC3H4 or INTS1 loss are subject to repression by these two factors under the experimental conditions.
source: This is consistent with the idea that they are subject to repression by these two factors under these experimental conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that upregulated transcripts are normally expressed at lower levels.

claim: Chromatin-associated RNA is purified via urea/detergent extraction and is enriched in nascent RNAs.
source: Chromatin-associated RNA is purified via urea/detergent extraction and is enriched in nascent RNAs (Wuarin and Schibler, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on chromatin-associated RNA purification.

claim: Integrator depletion reveals an accumulation of promoter-proximal RNAs in the coding direction consistent with its function as an attenuator of protein-coding transcription.
source: It also reveals an accumulation of promoter-proximal RNAs in the coding direction consistent with a recent report on its function as an attenuator of protein-coding transcription (Lykke-Andersen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by metagene analysis of chromatin-associated RNA-seq data and citation to a recent study on Integrator function.

claim: Previously published analyses of Integrator effects on transcription do not report the long extended non-coding (PROMPT/eRNA) transcripts observed when ZC3H4 is depleted.
source: Moreover, previously published analyses of Integrator effects on transcription do not report the long extended non-coding (PROMPT/eRNA) transcripts that we observe when ZC3H4 is depleted (Beckedorff et al., 2020; Lykke-Andersen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the current findings to previously published studies on Integrator.

claim: The timescale over which the effect of ZC3H4 depletion can be reversed suggests that transcripts induced by ZC3H4 loss remain relatively unstable.
source: The timescale over which the effect can be reversed suggests that transcripts induced by ZC3H4 loss remain relatively unstable.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the rapid reversal of ZC3H4 depletion effects upon TMP re-administration, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Some mRNAs are immediately and selectively upregulated following ZC3H4 loss.
source: This demonstrates that some mRNAs are immediately and selectively upregulated following ZC3H4 loss.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data on chromatin-associated RNA showing increased mRNA levels after 4 hr ZC3H4 depletion, as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The width of the ZC3H4 peak often corresponds to the normal extent of PROMPT and eRNA transcription, which is elongated in its absence.
source: The width of this peak often corresponds to the normal extent of PROMPT and eRNA transcription, which is elongated in its absence.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of ZC3H4 ChIP-seq occupancy patterns to the extent of PROMPT and eRNA transcripts observed in RNA-seq experiments.

claim: Flag-ZC3H4 occupies a subset of Pol II-bound regions and shows broader distribution than Pol II around promoters in HEPG2 cells.
source: Consistent with our findings, flag-ZC3H4 occupies a subset of Pol II-bound regions and shows broader distribution than Pol II around promoters (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of ENCODE ChIP-seq data for flag-ZC3H4 in HEPG2 cells, as shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Bioinformatics assignment of flag-ZC3H4 binding sites yielded 'promoter and enhancer-like' as the most enriched terms.
source: In further agreement with our data, bioinformatics assignment of flag-ZC3H4 binding sites yielded 'promoter and enhancer-like' as the most enriched terms (Partridge et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the ENCODE study that performed bioinformatic analysis of ZC3H4 binding sites.

claim: The consequences of ZC3H4 recruitment to targets are predicted to be their early termination and subsequent degradation by the exosome.
source: The consequences of ZC3H4 recruitment to targets are predicted to be their early termination and subsequent degradation by the exosome, based on the known fate of PROMPTs and eRNAs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known fate of PROMPTs and eRNAs and the effects of ZC3H4 depletion.

claim: Reporter RNA from the MS2hp-IRES-GFP construct is unaffected by endogenous ZC3H4.
source: Importantly, RNA from this reporter is unaffected by endogenous ZC3H4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing no change in reporter RNA levels following ZC3H4 depletion, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nascent RNAs associated with transfected plasmids co-purify within the chromatin-associated RNA fraction.
source: However, nascent RNAs associated with transfected plasmids also co-purify within this fraction (Dye et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on chromatin-associated RNA from transfected plasmids.

claim: Poly(A) site cleavage is co-transcriptional.
source: Because poly(A) site cleavage is co-transcriptional, this primer set should robustly detect Pol II-associated transcripts.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the timing of poly(A) site cleavage.

claim: The exosome degrades released PROMPT and eRNA transcripts.
source: The exosome degrades released PROMPT and eRNA transcripts, which could be enabled by ZC3H4.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about exosome function and inference about ZC3H4's role.

claim: ZC3H4 may regulate the stability of its targets.
source: ZC3H4 may also regulate the stability of its targets; however, to our knowledge, it has not been found to prominently co-purify with the exosome.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the lack of evidence for direct ZC3H4-exosome interaction.

claim: Multiple early termination pathways may contribute to conditional gene regulation.
source: An exciting possibility is that multiple early termination pathways may contribute to conditional gene regulation.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the discovery of multiple termination pathways including ZC3H4 and Integrator.

claim: ZC3H4 and/or Integrator may be naturally utilised to regulate transcription during development or across cell types.
source: It will be important to establish whether ZC3H4 and/or Integrator are naturally utilised to regulate transcription in this manner.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential biological roles of ZC3H4 and Integrator.

claim: The predominance of ZC3H4 and Integrator in metazoans may enable gene regulation across cell types or during development.
source: Their predominance in metazoans may enable gene regulation, for example across cell types or during development.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the metazoan-specific nature of ZC3H4 and Integrator.

claim: There is no known catalytic activity for ZC3H4 or Su(s).
source: There is no known catalytic activity for ZC3H4 or Su(s), but they are related to CPSF30 which shows endonuclease activity in Drosophila and Arabidopsis (Addepalli and Hunt, 2007; Bai and Tolias, 1996).
evidence: The claim is based on current knowledge about ZC3H4 and Su(s) and citation to studies on CPSF30 catalytic activity.

claim: It remains to be seen whether ZC3H4 possesses any catalytic activity or mediates its effects through interaction partners.
source: It remains to be seen whether ZC3H4 possesses any catalytic activity or mediates its effects through interaction partners.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the mechanism of ZC3H4 function.

claim: ZC3H4 may be recruited to promoter-proximal regions through WDR82 binding to Pol II phosphorylated on Serine 5 of its C-terminal domain.
source: WDR82 has been shown to bind to Pol II phosphorylated on Serine 5 of its C-terminal domain, which may provide a means to recruit ZC3H4 to promoter-proximal regions (Lee and Skalnik, 2008).
evidence: The claim is speculative based on known WDR82 function and its interaction with ZC3H4.

claim: ZC3H4 might control the escape of promoter-proximally paused polymerases or act closer to the 3' end of its target transcripts.
source: This might be by controlling the escape of promoter-proximally paused polymerases or by acting closer to the 3' end of its target transcripts.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the mechanism by which ZC3H4 restricts transcription.

claim: Elements of specificity such as sequences within DNA or RNA may explain ZC3H4's selective action.
source: The fact that ZC3H4 acts somewhat selectively (e.g. not all PROMPTs and mRNAs are its targets) suggests that elements of specificity are required to explain its mechanism. Most obviously, this could be sequences within DNA or RNA, to which ZC3H4 (and Su(s)) binds via ChIP and XRNAX, respectively (see Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the selective effects of ZC3H4 and its ability to bind DNA and RNA.

claim: It will be important to delineate any sequence determinants for ZC3H4 binding to its target transcripts.
source: Our evidence that ZC3H4 binds RNA in cells suggests that it may directly interact with some of its target transcripts and it will be important to delineate any sequence determinants.
evidence: The claim is speculative about future research directions.

claim: ZC3H4 may offer a new way to study enhancer clusters, particularly the importance of restricting transcription across these regions.
source: In general, ZC3H4 may offer a new way to study enhancer clusters, particularly the importance of restricting transcription across these regions.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential applications of ZC3H4 research.

claim: Further dissection of ZC3H4 and its targeting should reveal additional important insights into how the unstable portion of the transcriptome is controlled.
source: Further dissection of ZC3H4 and its targeting should reveal additional important insights into how the unstable portion of the transcriptome is controlled.
evidence: The claim is speculative about future research directions and potential insights.

claim: Multiple factors may control gene output via premature transcriptional termination.
source: The non-overlapping effects of Integrator and ZC3H4 at protein-coding genes indicate the possibility that multiple factors may control gene output via premature transcriptional termination.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that Integrator and ZC3H4 affect different sets of genes.
